content:
I am a data engineer,
I was thinking of ways to improve documentation, especially code to natural language translation and make code reviews easier.

A good analogy that most mathematicians won't know, is the dbt ecosystem around SQL language, were they also developed compilation mechanisms, tests and macros, and are now mature thanks to good IDE extensions like this one.

https://github.com/AltimateAI/vscode-dbt-power-user
You can generate documentation and visualize lineage of SQL code with that one.

dbt also has an HTML documentation generator that would more to be suggested to elan CLI maintainers.

In a thread on GitHub I was discussing this and people complaining that there are two many PRs opened to be reviewed, I also did this with Claude
https://commutator-io.github.io/mathlib4-review-helper/

I was wondering if you would like it as a VSCode extension, and what features you might find interesting.

It would litterrally less than 30 min for Claude to build that, considering we have open source examples and ideas in conversations on Zulip and GitHub to feed the AI coding assistant.
Hello! Could you explain what you're talking about and what are the features of what you've build and/or wanting to build, possibly with screenshots?

@Snir Broshi the second link has an example
https://commutator-io.github.io/mathlib4-review-helper/mycaule/pr/44756.html

I was thinking of migrating that experience to VSCode directly, since you can integrate well to GitHub in this IDE already.
(I'm asking because I don't want to click random links)
trying yourself is better than words, it just javascript hosted on github..

Most websites are essentially "just javascript", but you still shouldn't click any link.
I still suggest sharing info here, in case others are like-minded.

Right part doesn't exist currently, to my understanding, and GitHub provides GET URLs to create issues or add comments from an external tool.
Some of the review suggestions might be handled by handled by CodeRabbit and GitHub Code Review, though I don't have paid license to try.

For dbt it's a well known library, I let you investigate their philosophy, the links are safe :slight_smile:

Cool, thanks for sharing! (btw I know what dbt is, although I don't see how it's similar)

Personally I think we should review the code rather than the text, and I worry the text would distract from the contents of the PR. Note that there have been many previous attempts to show LLM summaries of theorems, in the docs of LLM-generated projects and in semantic search engines, where they seem to be more at home.

As for suggestions for a hypothetical review UI: I think being able to step through the proof similar to Verso, but with syntax highlighting and seeing diffs of the state like in the infoview, seems very useful to me.
Also I'd love to be able see the variables/opens/namespaces at any declaration (like #where shows), and see suggestions for better placement (such as #find_home, but also within the same file if there are similar theorems) if any.

So the idea of Verso is documentation generation and adding lots of comments to write the theorems in plain English just like Python docstring right ?

For dbt probably you haven't been using the dbt Power User extension to know, but it would not be a good idea if people are reluctant to installing more JS extensions, that are not maintained by lean-community.
No sorry I meant the example in their homepage of how proofs render: search for "theorem cantor" on the homepage and hover over the small ellipses between tactics.

What VSCode calls "language server" for the hovering stuff.

Another problem of LeanInfoView is that it's very hard to build the whole mathlib4 packages while reviewing only small pull requests. You have similar problems with dbt where you would only review small SQL models and do partial dbt compile or dbt run.


This kind of static analysis would also be helpful but doesn't exist for LEAN yet (similar to what pylint does for Python). Specific styleguide for mathlib4 contributors would also be useful.

Yeah in VSCode this is provided by the language-server, but the Lean ecosystem uses "infotrees", which is probably what Verso extracts (but I haven't checked, it could theoretically use the language server).

btw to answer your first question, I much prefer a website (that doesn't require a GitHub login) over a VSCode extension

I asked the last active maintainer of queueboard if we wanted to improve as well.
https://leanprover-community.github.io/queueboard/

This website is still suggested in pull requests from new contributors as a reminder.

Lineage graph in dbt models as a reminder, I guess we have tree graph for theorems, definitions as well.

Michel Hua said:

This kind of static analysis would also be helpful but doesn't exist for LEAN yet (similar to what pylint does for Python). Specific styleguide for mathlib4 contributors would also be useful.

We have lots of linters, and a style guide.
There have been previous attempts to write fancy prompts trying to find issues that reviewers often comment on, but they haven't been very successful AFAIK. (mathlib-conventions, mathlib-quality, lean-skills)

Then why is lean4 styleguide warnings not catched by GitHub Actions ?
For coding conventions if they don't live in the mathlib4 repo, people won't use them.
Because not every rule in the style guide is enforced by a linter.
(Also, note that the Lean prover itself and mathlib are different things. You seem to be mixing these up.)

I know the difference, what I wanted to point out is lean, the language, has a styleguide that mathlib4 should follow, but mathlib4 the library doesn't have a specific library level styleguide and people on PRs keep commenting their coding style the way they would like to be.

As Snir Broshi said people have been able to extract lots of ways to do and style preferences in the PRs (see Vilin97/mathlib-conventions)
That's incorrect: https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/style.html literally says "mathlib" at the top. is the mathlib style guide.

Oh gosh... I left maths many years ago, I forgot how some maths teacher were haha..
So if a PR is 100% OK against LEAN4 or Mathlib styleguide, I should just ignore the remaining style comments of the reviewers ?
Err, no: like with any reviewer comment, you should follow them or argue why you think it should be done otherwise.

It's hard to see who has strong and legit opinions on code style to be honest in the PRs,
TBH didn't know till today who Snir was, and I checked it he's the top 1 contributor of mathlib...

Sometimes people ask for things in the PR and then change their minds.
For example the other day I was proving the formula for the volume of a cone in 3D, someone asked me to prove it in any integer dimension, then d (non integer), then change their mind.

:sweat_smile: If you change the period at the top-right to "all" you'll see that there are lots of other great people above (and below) :)
(and this isn't even counting mathlib3)

Analogy with SQL and dbt is interesting, it's basically a very annoying language and tooling has made it very powerful and easy to use.

Plus SQL in build around theory of sets, just like the foundation of modern maths haha.

It's also funny to see that one of the actual top contributors over a longer period of time was actually one of my assistant teacher 20 years ago.
